C0.quote: define the winner of the vote using the deepest point of the scatter plot
C0.note: Grading-based voting rules aggregating voters' grades into a winner.

C1.quote: Neutrality, Universality, Unanimity, Monotonicity, and IIA
C1.note: Mostly property satisfaction/violation results and paradoxes; small remark on manipulability without formal analysis.

C2.1.quote: The grading is summarized in a d × n grading matrix

C2.2.quote: Approval voting is a voting process based on a binary set of grades.
C2.2.note: Grades in [0,1], discrete, continuous or binary.

C2.3.quote: the deepest point is a location estimator of the preferences of the voters
C2.3.note: Refers to voters' preferences and intensity of preferences.

C2.4.quote: the deepest point is a location estimator of the preferences of the voters
C2.4.note: Grades treated as preferences, rule applied directly with no statement about reporting.

C3.1.note: Strategic voting only mentioned informally (Sec 5 on large p, Sec 4.4 breakdown point).

C3.2.note: The no-show paradox definition mentions voting sincerely, but there is no statement that voters submit their held attitude.

C4.1.note: Input is cardinal grades only; no ordinal/approval input linked to separate utilities, so applicability condition not met (approval is a special case of grades).

C5.1.note: Evaluates axiomatic properties and paradoxes; Condorcet paradoxes are not welfare/efficiency criteria as defined.

VOT.note: Voters supply grades as fixed data; no actions modelled.

claims.quote: Grading-based voting offers a richer information than ranking-based model.
The fact that a voting process elects c2 is acceptable in this configuration.
which means that the procedure is less manipulable.

C9.1.note: Claims about which rules/properties are desirable and acceptability of paradoxes.

C9.2.note: Claims about manipulability and about acceptable paradoxes need assumptions about voter behaviour and grades reflecting held preferences/intensity, which are not stated.
